author: Hannah Arendt
introFa: کتاب «The Human Condition» نوشته Hannah Arendt یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C2 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.

One way of understanding the central message of Arendt’s politics is, therefore, that societies that fail to understand the differences between action and fabrication will also fail to understand the difference between power and violence. Only power can act on the boundlessness of action, and ‘impotence breeds violence’ (Arendt, 1971: 54). The irreversibility and unpredictability of action are discussed at the end of the chapter on ‘Action’ in The Human Condition. Both relate to what Arendt calls the ‘process character of action’. She writes: While the strength of the production process is entirely absorbed in and exhausted by the end product, the strength of the action process is never exhausted in a single deed but, on the contrary, can grow while its consequences multiply; what endures in the realm of human affairs are [only] these processes. . . . The reason why we are never able to foretell with certainty the outcome and end of any action is simply that action has no end. . . . The very meaning [of a deed or event] never discloses itself to the actor but only to the backward glance of the historian. (Arendt, 1998: 233) Action then, as opposed to labor or fabrication, has a capacity to expand beyond the ini- tial web of relations to which the original actor intended to direct it. This gives action its irreversible and unpredictable qualities. The irreversibility and unpredictability of action can be mitigated by the human powers of forgiveness and promising respectively. These are related and complementary capacities. Forgiveness offers no route ‘backwards’ beyond the actuality of an action, but has the capacity to break up the process engendered by it, and to negate the will to vengeance (ibid.: 240), and thus allow new beginnings. The capacity for promising plays into the unpredictability of action by creating ‘islands of certainty’ in the ocean of the future. Both capacities have primarily political – rather than simply moral – significance, insofar as their sphere of influence lies within the realm of action. One need not accept that the emergent properties of action that Arendt cites are exhaustive, or conceptually unproblematic, to take them seriously as significant contri- butions to an understanding of both order and change within human societies. It is also striking how much the concepts of irreversibility, unpredictability and boundlessness have come to the fore in recent attempts to theorize the impact of new scientific knowl- edge and technology on the dynamics of advanced industrialized societies. In the final section, I argue that Arendt’s ontological distinction between fabrication and action can also be applied – at least in principle – to understanding the impact of new technologies, and as an augmentation of existing approaches to the issue. Action, Knowledge and Technology There is a widespread ‘Tocquevillean’ interpretation of Arendt that takes her to be arguing that action is increasingly unavailable in modern society, as a result of the ‘rise of the social’ and the subordination of politics to social and economic concerns (see, for example, D’Entre`ves, 1994: 49–50). This interpretation confuses the realm of politics with the ontological category of action in general. In fact, Arendt suggests not only that 130 History of the Human Sciences 24(2) at Swinburne Univ of Technology on May 16, 2015 hhs.sagepub.com

the realm of action itself cannot be destroyed (1998: 230), but that – in contrast to her claim that the realm of fabrication is shrinking through the reduction of work to labor – the realm of action in the modern world seems to be expanding. This growth of action is partly due to the increasing exercise of human power over the natural world, which alters the human condition in fundamental ways. This is the point behind Arendt’s obser- vation that modern technological science increasingly appears as an ‘acting into nature’, rather than an act of making. It is important to be aware how decisively the technological world we live in, or perhaps begin to live in, differs from the mechanized world as it arose with the Industrial Revolu- tion. This difference corresponds essentially to the difference between action and fabrica- tion. Industrialization still consisted primarily of the mechanization of work processes, the improvement in the making of objects, and man’s attitude to nature still remained that of homo faber, to whom nature gives the material out of which the human artifice is erected. The world we have come to live in, however, is much more determined by man acting into nature, creating natural processes and directing them into the human artifice and the realm of human affairs. (Arendt, 1961: 59) Arendt’s primary example of such ‘acting into nature’ was the invention of the atomic bomb, and the political structures that arose to govern its consequences. However, her conception of the unprecedentedness of ‘acting into nature’ is underdeveloped. In the few attempts she made to specify a clear distinction between ‘technologies of fabrica- tion’ and ‘technologies of action’, she fastens on the point that the latter produce effects that otherwise would not occur (see 1961: 58) and it is difficult to see this in itself as a valid marker, since the same thing could be said of a range of industrial processes that go beyond the classification of the ‘improvement in the making of objects’ (think, for exam- ple, of the industrial development of plastics in the 1930s–1950s). The key distinction between the two kinds of technology is to be found instead in the last clause of the above quotation. Certain technologies, because they affect the mode of comportment in which human beings confront ‘the given’ of their existence on Earth, directly impact the very basis of their social and the political worlds. They thereby become part of the realm of action, and start to exhibit its distinct emergent properties, especially unpredictability and boundlessness, as well as becoming subject to various forms of political contesta- tion. The effects of the ‘action character’ of the technology of atomic weaponry can be seen quite dramatically in the startling and unprecedented proliferation of institutions that it spawned in the United States in the 1950s and 1960s.13 But this character is now also visible in a range of newer technologies that have the potential to impact very sig- nificantly the social and political basis of human relationships. Examples of such tech- nologies include molecular biology, synthetic genomics, other biotechnologies oriented to human enhancement, bio-weaponry, some lines of research associated with technolo- gically assisted reproduction and new psycho-pharmacological products.14 Of course, the potential dangers of such technologies are widely recognized, and are addressed in the form of ethics boards, professional norms and law at the state and trans- national levels, with more or less effectiveness, depending on your point of view, the technology, the authority and legitimacy of the regulating institution and a host of other Walsh 131 at Swinburne Univ of Technology on May 16, 2015 hhs.sagepub.com

factors. But Arendt’s observation about the unprecedented action character of modern technology is a more general one: there is an overall tendency for technologically oriented science increasingly to resemble action more than fabrication, and, given the increasing influence of science, this extends the field of action in general. The continuing expansion of human knowledge can therefore be expected to introduce greater uncer- tainty, unpredictability and boundlessness into the realm of human affairs. The position of scientific knowledge within the human artifice, in other words, has been transformed from that of a tool for the prediction and control of nature, in the hands of Homo faber, to being itself a form of action and therefore a source of unpredictability and uncontrollable effects. Arendt’s insights here again converge more closely with sociologists than with phi- losophers or political theorists. In particular, theorists of the ‘risk society’ and ‘knowl- edge society’ have arrived at very similar conclusions to Arendt concerning the transformed and transforming role of scientific knowledge within human societies.15 Thus, the originator of the concept of risk society, Ulrich Beck, has pointed out that ‘the category of risk society reflects the response to uncertainty, which nowadays often can- not be overcome by more knowledge but is instead a result of more knowledge’ (Beck, 2009: 5). Similarly, Nico Stehr, who has advanced the idea of ‘knowledge society’ as an ideal type descriptor of advanced technologically oriented societies, observes that ‘in contrast to past disputes, when discussions of the societal consequences of science were driven by complaints about its deficient social and economic utility . . . today concern is increasingly directed toward a surplus of effects – especially with respect to . . . the lim- its of what may be manipulated in nature and society’ (2004: xi–xii). The convergence of these models with Arendt’s concerns is also apparent in both Beck’s and Stehr’s insis- tence that the emergence of new forms of knowledge and technology will increasingly put pressure on our social and political institutions, and has led them, among others, to emphasize the increasing need for knowledge governance at the societal level, i.e. to develop a knowledge politics that recognizes the novelty of our current dilemmas vis-a`-vis scientific knowledge, and a set of political principles to deal with them. How could Arendt’s insights into the ‘action character’ of scientific knowledge inform the models of knowledge governance that have been proposed? The most striking feature of most contemporary knowledge governance models is their tendency to treat scientific knowledge either as a tool or as a commodity.16 Both approaches assume that knowledge can therefore be handled in the same way we treat the means of production and the products of human labor, and can be regulated in the same way – in the mode of fabrication rather than as action. Arendt’s theory of action points to the dangers of such an approach: it fails to take account of the unpredictability, irreversibility and boundlessness of action, and rests on a faulty ontology of scientific knowledge. A more promising proposal, which is aligned quite closely with Arendt’s perspective, and incorporates the basic insights of both risk- and knowledge-society the- ory, is Steve Fuller’s ‘civic Republican’ approach to knowledge governance. Fuller’s model involves two key elements. First, is the reassertion of the university as the key site of knowledge production, and as an exemplar of the public sphere. Second, is the insti- tutionalization of ‘consensus conferences’ involving citizen juries. Citizens are thereby brought into the process of establishing the priorities for funding scientific research and 132 History of the Human Sciences 24(2) at Swinburne Univ of Technology on May 16, 2015 hhs.sagepub.com

adjudicating national science policies (2006: 164–71; 2007: 109–14). The goal of consensus conferences is not in fact consensus, but only ‘the parameters for subsequent deliberation and action’ (2006: 165) concerning science policy. Indeed, Fuller advocates against a regulative ideal of ‘right policy’, and – acknowledging many of the principles of risk- and knowledge-society theorists – asserts that the goal of science governance policy should not be certainty but the reversibility of such decisions that are made, i.e. that acknowledges the fact that no ‘right’ decision might be available. Fuller’s proposals are more complex and detailed than I have suggested here, but his insistence on the need for a public sphere in the governance of science has a striking resonance with Arendt’s political perspective. It points to a need to integrate Arendt’s theories of power, action and knowledge, understood ontologically in the manner pro- posed above, into current debates about the governance of knowledge. Conclusion Arendt’s insights into the distinctions between labor, work and action can be fruitfully reinterpreted as a general theory of ‘society’. This would incorporate a stratified and dif- ferentiated social ontology, with emergent properties attached to the different spheres of activity. It is not necessarily a reinterpretation that Arendt would herself support, given her hostility to the social sciences and the theories of ‘society’ that she encountered in her own time. Nevertheless, notwithstanding the concentration of recent commentators on Arendt’s overtly political writings, Arendt’s work is more influential within the social sciences today than it has ever been. A rapprochement between Arendt and sociology therefore seems long overdue. This article has shown how we could begin to go about accomplishing this, and suggested one way in which this reinterpretation might inform recent social theoretical insights into the changing character of knowledge and technology. This state of affairs with respect to knowledge may therefore be said to be historically unpre- cedented, which raises important further considerations. The problem of unprecedentedness has been explored in detail by Peter Baehr’s studies of Arendt’s theory of totalitarianism (Baehr, 2002, 2010). He asks, can there be unprecedented events? And to what extent can such events be grasped by political and social scientists in ways that would allow us to confront them and deal with their consequences more adequately?
